Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette: Kofi had always been drawn to the field of psychology, fascinated by the complexities of the human mind. As a successful psychologist in his late 30s, he had built a thriving practice helping others navigate their own traumas and struggles. But it was an irony that wasn't lost on him - Kofi's own life had been forever altered by a traumatic event that still lingered, unspoken, like a shadow. It happened during his graduate school days, when he was in his mid-20s. A night out with friends at a local bar had ended with him stumbling back to his apartment, alone and drunk. He vaguely recalled letting someone in - a acquaintance from the bar - who then attacked and raped him. The details were hazy, but the aftermath was all too clear: the shame, the guilt, the overwhelming sense of powerlessness. In the months that followed, Kofi found himself increasingly withdrawn. Simple tasks became daunting challenges. He would find excuses to avoid social gatherings or meetings with colleagues, afraid of being alone with men - a constant reminder of his own vulnerability. Comments about sexual violence, whether in the news or casual conversation, left him reeling. It was as if every word cut through him like a knife. As a psychologist, Kofi knew intellectually that he wasn't responsible for what had happened. But emotionally, he couldn't shake off the feeling of helplessness - that he'd been unable to stop the attack, and now, nothing seemed safe anymore. He felt exposed, as if others could see right through him, somehow sensing the trauma he'd endured. Kofi's daily routine became a minefield of triggers. Confined spaces made his skin crawl; elevators were especially unbearable. Even his own apartment, once a sanctuary, now felt suffocating. At night, he would lie awake for hours, vigilant and alert, certain that he needed to stay on guard against some unknown threat. The only place where Kofi could momentarily feel at ease was his office - but even there, the walls seemed to close in when clients came in. His back always found its way to the wall, instinctively seeking a vantage point from which he could survey the room, like a sentry on high alert. As time went by, these habits began to erode Kofi's relationships and work performance. Colleagues noticed his increased irritability; friends grew concerned about his social isolation. Patients sensed his tension during sessions, making it harder for him to connect with them on a deeper level. It was as if he'd lost himself in the process of trying to cope. Kofi knew that he needed help - not just for others, but for himself. The final straw came when he realized he couldn't even bear to listen to his patients' stories without feeling overwhelmed by his own memories. He began questioning whether he had a future as a psychologist at all; the shame and hopelessness threatened to consume him. Now, Kofi sits in a therapist's office, hoping against hope that someone can help him unravel this tangled web of emotions and fears. For the first time in years, he feels willing to confront the shadows head-on - not just for his own sake, but so he can regain the passion and purpose that once drove him to become a psychologist in the first place.
